Title screen, story scroller and the way into a game, called by the restart at $0818 before every game. Gives $0314 back to the KERNAL ($EA31) and turns the raster interrupt off, blanks the screen, switches all sprites off, points the story scroller at its text ($5E4C/$5E4D = $8009), makes border and background black, prints CHR$(8) (SHIFT and C= may no longer switch the character set) and CHR$(147) (clears the text screen at $0400) through CHROUT, clears colour RAM to black and fills it with the picture's colours from $AC00-$AFFE (copy_block with the parameters at $5E44), starts tune 0, the main theme (music_init with A = 0), installs title_irq ($5D08) for raster $30 with $5E4A = 0 and turns the screen on. Clears $03D3 (what the game about to start does with the controls: 0 play, 1 record a demonstration, 2 play the demonstration back) and $03D9 (a pass of the story has ended), then waits in title_wait_loop.

Title loop. CTRL held on its own with R ($028D = 4 and key code $C5 = $11) waits for CTRL to be let go, sets $03D3 = 1 (the game about to start records the controls as a demonstration) and saves the random seed $0383/$0384 at $A540/$A541, the head of the demonstration buffer. When the story has scrolled through once ($03D9 set by title_scroll_step) it sets $03D3 = 2 (the game plays the demonstration back). Otherwise it polls the controls ($179D: joystick port 2 and keys; M switches the music) and on fire or SPACE ($0387) waits 5 units ($0F35), waits for the release, waits 5 more and leaves with $03D3 = 0.

Leaving the title: blanks the screen, stops the music (music_stop, then music_play to silence it at once), gives $0314 back to the KERNAL ($EA31) and sets up the character screen the play screen's top band uses: multicolour character mode, 40 columns, $D018 = $1D (screen $0400, characters $3000), bitmap mode off, VIC bank 0 ($DD00 bits 0-1 = %11), raster interrupt off; border light blue, background black, $D022 red, $D023 light grey; screen on. With $03D3 non-zero (recording or playing back a demonstration) it returns at once and the game starts. Otherwise it prints the controls page from $838E (CHROUT loop $2BC7) and polls: B or the stick pulled down ($0389 = 1) goes to title_instructions, fire starts the game after a whole press (wait_fire_press).

The instructions reached with B from the controls page: five pages printed through CHROUT from $84B7 (HOW TO CONTROL THE GAME), $86E7 (THE DISPLAY), $8893 (TO PLAY THE GAME), $8B1B (USING MAGIC) and $8DB1 (MAGICAL OR PHYSICAL COMBAT), each ended by a whole press of fire (wait_fire_press); after the fifth the game starts.

Block copy. X/Y (low, high) point at a 6-byte parameter block of three addresses, low byte first: source start (to $9B/$9C), source end (to $9D/$9E) and destination (to $63/$64). Copies a byte at a time, upwards, until the source pointer equals the end, so the end byte itself is not copied. Callers: title_screen with $5E44 ($AC00-$AFFE into colour RAM at $D800) and $0AB8 in the game setup with $57DD ($A858-$A9FE into colour RAM at $DA58). Changes A, X, Y, $63/$64 and $9B-$9E.

Title raster interrupt, entered through $0314 from the KERNAL's $FF48 with A, X and Y already pushed. Acknowledges the VIC ($D019 written back). An interrupt without the raster flag, which can only be CIA 1's timer, returns straight away without reading $DC0D: the CIA keeps asking and the handler is re-entered until the scroller half's KERNAL exit reads $DC0D (traced, not observed). Two halves alternate on $5E4A: 0 the picture half at raster $30 (title_irq_picture), 1 the scroller half at raster $EE (title_irq_scroller, reached through a JMP to the next instruction at $5D1D).

Scroller half of title_irq, at raster $EE (inside character row 23): hires character mode in VIC bank 0 (multicolour and bitmap off, $D018 = $1D: screen $0400, characters $3000, $DD00 bits 0-1 = %11), next interrupt at raster $30 with $5E4A = 0, 38 columns with the fine scroll $5E4B as $D016's X scroll so the story in row 24 ($07C0) slides left; then one frame of music ($1949, which calls music_play) and out through the KERNAL's $EA31 (jiffy clock, keyboard scan, $DC0D read).

Picture half of title_irq, at raster $30 (just above the display window): VIC bank 3 ($DD00 bits 0-1 = %00), next interrupt at raster $EE, multicolour bitmap mode with $D018 = $38 (screen matrix $CC00, title_screen_matrix; bitmap $E000-$FF3F in the RAM under the KERNAL), 40 columns and no X scroll, $5E4A = 1; then two steps of the story (title_scroll_step twice, two pixels a frame) and returns without the KERNAL.

One pixel of the story scroller, called twice a frame by the picture half. On NTSC ($02A6 = 0) the countdown $03DA, reloaded with 2, skips every second call, so the story moves one pixel a frame there (60 a second) against two on PAL (100 a second). Decrements the fine scroll $5E4B; below 0 it becomes 7, the text pointer $5E4C/$5E4D moves on a character and row 24 is redrawn: 40 bytes from the pointer to $07C0-$07E7, those from $40 to $BF less $40 (PETSCII letters to screen codes), the rest unchanged, all yellow ($DBC0-$DBE7 = 7). When the pointer reaches $8366, after 861 characters (68.9 s on PAL), it goes back to $8009, $03D9 = 2 tells title_wait_loop to start the demonstration, and the random seed $0383/$0384 is reloaded from $A540/$A541 ($F8, $18), so the demonstration starts from the seed its recording started from. Only this end of a whole pass reloads the seed: a game started from the title keeps the seed the last game or demonstration left.

Waits for a whole press of fire or SPACE: polls the controls ($179D) until $0387 is set, waits 5 units ($0F35), polls until it is released, waits 5 more. Used by the controls and instruction pages and at the end of a game ($08AA).

Story scroller's fine X scroll, counting 7 down to 0, put into $D016 bits 0-2 by the scroller half; below 0 it goes back to 7 and the text moves on a character. title_screen does not reset it, so a new title starts at the offset the last one stopped at.

CBM80 HEADER, $8000-$8008, word 1: the cold-start vector, $0818, the game's restart (the title and demonstration, then a new game). With the signature at $8004 in place the KERNAL's reset routine jumps through this word instead of starting BASIC, so a reset restarts the game (live, features.md). Loaded with the game; no game code reads or writes $8000-$8008. The game's own title code takes its text from $8009, straight after the header, so the header is probably part of the original layout rather than the crack's.

CBM80 header word 2: the warm-start vector, also $0818. The KERNAL's NMI handler finds the signature and jumps through this word when RESTORE is pressed, so RESTORE restarts the game at the title rather than breaking into BASIC (live, features.md).

CBM80 signature: $C3 $C2 $CD $38 $30, that is C, B and M with bit 7 set, then 8 and 0: the five bytes the KERNAL compares at reset and on RESTORE to decide that a cartridge is present and take the vectors at $8000/$8002. The game is not a cartridge; the signature is only there to catch reset and RESTORE.

When the pointer reaches $8366 it goes back to $8009 and sets $03D9 = 2, and the title loop ($5BE4) then starts the demonstration: one pass of this text is how long the title lasts unless fire is pressed. Dungeon map, $9000-$9FFF; this is row 0. 32 rows of 128 cells, one byte per cell: a character code of the top band's set at $3000, which the view window shows unchanged (colour from tile_colour, $A400), so the 11x11 window is an opening onto this map. Cell (row r, column c) is at $9000 + r*$80 + c, two rows per page; north is up the screen. The 128 columns hold four levels of 32 side by side (level 1: columns 0-31, 2: 32-63, 3: 64-95, 4: 96-127), and a staircase moves whoever steps onto its trigger half exactly 32 columns, to the same row of the next or previous level ($20CC). Every position the game keeps is an address in this map: the player's, each creature's and each object's ($3F70/$3FB0; a high byte of $00 means carried by entry nn instead) and the creatures' destinations ($4CAE/$4CCD). Codes: $7E rock and $7F (the view's unseen fill, also used for a few rock cells) are solid black; $91 is open floor; the other codes from $80 to $B9 are floor cells with mid-grey wall lines along some edges (room walls and corners, corridors, dead ends, cave edges); $B0 $B1 and $B2 $B3 are staircases and $A3 a one-way drop; $50-$53 and $70-$73 are pool water and its rim, $70 being the pedestal; $F0-$FF are doors, each door two cells facing each other across a wall: bit 0 set = open; bit 3 clear = the other half is a row away, set = one cell across; bit 1 clear = below or to the right, set = above or to the left; bit 2 only picks the glyph (a door in a room wall, or at the end of a narrow passage). Exits for door-opening creatures: one byte per character code ($00-$FF), indexed by the tile a creature stands on; bit n set lets it step out in direction n, 0 north then clockwise (1 north-east, 2 east, 3 south-east, 4 south, 5 south-west, 6 west, 7 north-west; the bit masks are at $4960, the opposite directions at $49F9). Identical to tile_exits at $A100 except for the closed doors $F0, $F2, $F4, $F6, $F8, $FA, $FC and $FE, which here also allow the direction through the door (e.g. $F0: $D7 here, $C7 there; the extra bit is south). The creature mover $2566 reads this table instead of $A100 when the creature's flag $5001,y is set: $2581 writes $A0 into $25A7, the operand high byte of its LDA $A100,y, and $2589 writes $A1 back otherwise. When $A100 ($25C6) then refuses the chosen direction, the creature opens the door ($2600 calls $1BBF) and closes it behind it on its next move ($25F4 calls $1C85). Entries for codes $00-$50 and for the marker figures $C0-$EF are 0. The table sits in the top rows of the bottom band's bitmap page, which the screen never shows.

Exits for every other creature: the table the mover $2566 reads by default, and the one it always checks a chosen direction against ($25C6). One byte per character code, bit n = may step out of a cell holding that code in direction n (0 north, clockwise to 7 north-west); closed doors refuse the direction through the door. The player's own moves are checked another way: a collision of the player's sprite with wall, rock or door pixels in the view ($D01F collected into $038D) makes $0AD3-$0ADF call $0F95, which reverses the direction of travel ($0388/$0389). This first quarter, codes $00-$3F (the text characters; the map holds only the digit labels $31, $33, $34, sealed in rock), is all 0.

The random-number state the recorded demonstration was made with, first byte: the value of $0383 (the index $2B9E reads $E000,x with, stepped +1 per number) when CTRL+R on the title screen started the recording ($5BD6), put back before every replay when the title scroller ends ($5DF2), so the dungeon's random events repeat exactly: $F8.
Second byte of the demonstration's random state: $0384, the index $2B9E reads $E800,y with (stepped -3 per number), saved at $5BDC and restored at $5DF8: $18.

Where the demonstration's input pointer $03D4/$03D5 starts ($0A7E-$0A85 set it to $A542 for every game). The recorder and the player both step the pointer before they write or read, and the first recorded state can never equal the initial state 7 in $03D6, so this byte ($0F) is never used; the stream begins at $A543.

The recorded demonstration: joystick input as run-length bytes, written by the recorder ($17AD-$1887, when $03D3 = 1) and replayed into $0387-$0389 by $1888-$1946 (when $03D3 = 2), one step per call of the input routine $179D. Each byte: high nibble = stick bits (1 east, 2 west, 4 south, 8 north, 0 none; $F = fire, $E = end), low nibble = polls - 1. The recorder stores each fire press as $FA (fire for 11 polls) and records nothing while fire stays held. This recording holds 5,308 polls of play (moves through the dungeon and the menus, 46 fire presses) to $A767, then 151 idle bytes $0F (16 polls each); the end byte $EF at $A7FF is what the recorder writes over its last byte when the buffer runs out at the limit $A800 ($1864-$187B; the limit is tested at $17E6, $1867 and the player's $1912), so by the idle run before it the recording was left to fill the buffer. F ($C5 = $15) ends a recording early.

Colour-RAM image of screen rows 15-24 ($A858 stands for colour RAM $DA58, row 15 column 0): the new-game setup copies $A858-$A9FE there ($0AB8 calls $5CC5 with the descriptor at $57DD; $A9FF is not copied). Screen matrix of the bottom band, rows 16-24 (VIC bank 2; band 2's interrupt sets $D018 = $A8 at $27E0, so matrix $A800 and bitmap $A000): each byte gives a bitmap cell's '01' colour (high nibble) and '10' colour (low nibble), its '11' colour coming from colour RAM. Only these rows are shown, because band 2 begins at raster $B6, inside character row 16; the page's upper rows hold other data. Row 16 ($AA80-$AAA7) is 0, the black strip under the menu band. In rows 17-24, columns 0-1 and 38-39 hold the pillars' colours (loaded, never changed) and columns 2-37 are the twelve picture slots, six cells wide and four rows high, six across in rows 17-20 and six in rows 21-24: $1515 copies a picture's colours in (slot destinations $57FB/$5807) and they stay behind when the picture goes, since $14C3 clears only the bitmap. Picture 0, the player's, which is never drawn, names $AA80 as its matrix source.
Sprite pointers of the bottom band's screen matrix ($A800 + $3F8): the new-game loop at $0A66-$0A7C sets all eight to $94, sprite_dead_label at $A500 ($8000 + $94 x 64); 0 in the loaded image.

Colour-RAM image of the title picture, 40 x 25 cells ($AC00-$AFE7; the rest is 0). The title setup copies $AC00-$AFFE to $D800 once ($5B82 calls $5CC5 with the descriptor at $5E44; $AFFF is not copied). The picture is a multicolour bitmap in VIC bank 3, shown by the title interrupt's upper phase ($5D63-$5D96: bitmap mode, $D018 = $38, so bitmap $E000 and matrix $CC00); each byte here is a cell's '11' colour: yellow $07 and brown $09 for the logo lettering in rows 0-10, dark grey $0B and white $01 for the cave, red $02 and blue $06 for the figure at columns 8-10, rows 13-17. Rows 23-24 are 0: from raster $EE the interrupt switches to text mode in bank 0 (screen $0400, characters $3000) for the scroller in row 24, whose colour $5E1A writes as yellow.

Bitmap row 16 of the bottom band ($A000 + 16 x 320), all 0. Band 2 begins at raster $B6, a few lines into character row 16, so the rest of this row shows as the black strip between the menu band and the pictures. Picture 0, the player's, which is never drawn, names $B400 as its bitmap source.

Bitmap row 17 ($B540-$B67F), the top row of the picture strip. Columns 0-1 ($B540-$B54F) and 38-39 ($B670-$B67F): the upper half of the skull that tops each pillar, loaded and never changed (the two pillars show the same picture, encoded with different colour choices). Columns 2-37 ($B550-$B66F): the top pixel rows of the six upper picture slots, drawn by $1515 from a picture's bitmap (slot destinations $57E3/$57EF) and cleared by $14C3; empty in the loaded image.
Bitmap row 18 ($B680-$B7BF): the lower half of each skull (columns 0-1 and 38-39); columns 2-37 ($B690-$B7AF) the second character row of the upper picture slots.

Bitmap row 19 ($B7C0-$B8FF): the top of each pillar's wooden pole and the snake's first coil round it (columns 0-1 and 38-39); columns 2-37 ($B7D0-$B8EF) the third character row of the upper picture slots.
Bitmap row 20 ($B900-$BA3F): pole and snake coil on each pillar (columns 0-1 and 38-39); columns 2-37 ($B910-$BA2F) the bottom character row of the upper six picture slots.

Bitmap row 21 ($BA40-$BB7F): pole and snake on each pillar; columns 2-37 ($BA50-$BB6F) the top character row of the lower six picture slots (the odd-numbered slots; a picture eight rows high takes an upper slot and the lower one beneath it).
Bitmap row 22 ($BB80-$BCBF): pole and snake on each pillar; columns 2-37 ($BB90-$BCAF) the second character row of the lower picture slots.
Bitmap row 23 ($BCC0-$BDFF): the foot of each pole with the snake's body; columns 2-37 ($BCD0-$BDEF) the third character row of the lower picture slots.

Bitmap row 24 ($BE00-$BF3F), the band's last: the snake's head with its open red mouth at the foot of each pillar (columns 0-1 and 38-39); columns 2-37 ($BE10-$BF2F) the bottom character row of the lower picture slots. The bitmap ends at $BF3F; $BF40-$BFFF is unused.

Music entry: start tune A (0 the main theme, 1 death, 2 won: the songs 1-3 of HVSC's Master_of_Magic.sid, 'Main Theme', 'Game Over (You're dead)' and 'Game beaten'). Jumps to music_start_tune ($CBC3). Called with A = 0 by the title ($5B8C), the start of every game ($0A94) and the M key ($0CBB); with A = 1 at the end of a game lost or of the demonstration ($086E) and with A = 2 at the end of a game won, $03C7 = $7B ($0861).

Music entry: stop. Jumps to music_request_stop ($CBE1), which sets the state $C41D to $C0; the next music_play silences all three voices. Called by the M key ($0CB0), by title_leave ($5C13) and by music_next_note when a track reaches its $FE ($C087).

Music entry: play one frame. Called once a frame through $1949, which on NTSC drops every sixth call to keep the PAL tempo: from title_irq's scroller half on the title, and in play from the menu band at raster $8E while $03D1 is on; also called straight after music_stop to silence at once. Counts frames in $C426, then acts on the state $C41D: $00 plays; $40 (set by music_start_tune) zeroes each voice's track position, pattern position, length counter and note, and the frame counter, sets $00 and plays; $C0 (set by music_stop) clears the three voices' control registers (waveform and gate off), sets the volume to 15 and the state to $80; $80 returns at once.

Plays the three voices, SID voice 3 first (X = 2, 1, 0; the voice's register offset from $C3EF into $C3F2). The tempo counter $C41A counts down and is reloaded from $C41B (1), and a tick, when notes move on, is the frame on which it equals $C41B: every second frame, 25 ticks a second on PAL. On a tick a voice whose length counter $C3F9 runs out (goes below 0) reads its next note (music_next_note); otherwise it goes through music_release and the effects. Between ticks only the effects (music_effects) run.
JMP $C328 that is never executed: it follows the JMP $C160 above and nothing jumps or branches to it.

A voice's next note, on the tick its length counter runs out. Reads the voice's track, through ($FB) = its address from $C4AF/$C4B2, at its track position $C3F3: $FF sends the track back to its start (track position, pattern position and length counter 0) and reads again; $FE stops the music (music_stop, then returns without playing the remaining voices this frame); any other value is the number of the pattern being played, 0-40, whose address comes from music_pattern_lo/hi ($C4C7/$C4F0) into ($FD).
JMP $C328 that is never executed: it follows the JMP $C07A above and nothing jumps or branches to it.

Reads a note from the pattern at the voice's pattern position $C3F6. First byte (into $C3FC and $C409): bits 0-4 the length in ticks less 1 (into the length counter $C3F9: 1-32 ticks, 0.04-1.28 s on PAL); bit 5 no release at the end (tied into the next note); bit 6 a rest: the byte stands alone and the voice's instrument is rewritten with the gate off for that length; bit 7 an instrument number follows (into $C405). Then the note number (into $C402), 0-95 for C0-B7, whose frequency from music_freq_lo/hi goes to the voice's frequency registers and to $C421/$C41E. Also sets the master volume $D418 on every note read: $75 less voice 3's track position ($C3F5), at most 15, which fades tune 0 out as its voice 3 goes through positions $67-$75.

Writes the voice's instrument ($C405; 8 bytes each in music_instruments, $C427 + 8n) to the SID: the control byte ANDed with the gate mask $C408 ($FF, or $FE for a rest) to $D404 + voice offset and kept in $C3FF, the pulse width to $D402/$D403, attack/decay and sustain/release to $D405/$D406. Then steps past the note; if the next byte is $FF the pattern has ended: pattern position 0, track position + 1.

On a tick while a note sounds: in its last tick (length counter 0), unless bit 5 of the note's first byte is set, turns the gate off and sets attack/decay and sustain/release to 0, so the note dies at the fastest release rate before the next one starts.

Every frame, the effects of the voice's instrument: fx flags (instrument byte 7) into $C424, pulse speed (byte 6) into $C40E, vibrato depth (byte 5) into $C40D. Vibrato, when the depth is not 0: the frequency becomes the note's plus phase x (the next semitone's - the note's) / 2^(depth+1), the phase running 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 0 with the frame counter $C426, a wobble upwards only; on notes of 4 ticks or fewer the phase is not added and the note's own frequency is written.

Pulse width effects. fx bit 3: the pulse speed is added to the instrument's pulse width low byte every frame and written to $D402 (there is no CLC, so a carry left from the vibrato can add one more). Otherwise, with a pulse speed other than 0, a sweep: every (speed AND $1F) + 1 frames (timer $C414 per voice) the 12-bit pulse width moves by speed AND $E0, up until its high nibble reaches $E, then down until it reaches 8 (direction $C417 per voice); the value goes to $D402/$D403 and back into the instrument, which keeps it for the next time it plays.

fx bit 0, the drum: while the frequency high byte $C41E and the length counter are both non-zero, in the note's first tick the waveform is noise with the gate off ($80); after that the frequency high byte drops by one every frame, with the instrument's own waveform and the gate off. Instruments 4, 7, 14 and 16 also have the octave arpeggio, which rewrites the frequency after this every frame, so only instrument 11's pitch actually falls.

fx bit 1, a fall at the end of long notes: on notes of 17 ticks or more, while the length counter is below 18, on every odd frame (frame counter $C426) the frequency high byte $C41E is written to the SID and lowered by one, until it is 0. Only instrument 12 has it (pattern 20, tune 0); its vibrato writes the note's own frequency every frame first, so the voice alternates frame by frame between the note and the falling pitch.

fx bit 2, an octave arpeggio: on 7 frames out of 8 (frame counter AND 7 not 0) the voice plays the note an octave up (note + 12), on the eighth the note itself. Pattern 34 plays note 91 (G7) with instrument 16, and note 103 lies past the 96-entry table: its frequency is read from the driver's variables at $C3FD/$C3FE.
Next voice (X down to 0), then returns to the caller of music_play.

Note frequency table: 96 notes from C0 (note 0) to B7 (note 95), two bytes each, low byte first; the driver reads note n's low byte at $C32F + 2n. Tuned for PAL (985,248 Hz): A4, note 57, is $1D46 = 440.1 Hz, and notes 0-94 lie within 3.2 cents of equal temperament; an NTSC machine plays them about 65 cents (two thirds of a semitone) sharp. This byte: the low byte of C0 ($0116, 16.3 Hz).
High byte of note 0, C0; the driver reads note n's high byte at $C330 + 2n (note start and octave effect).
Low byte of note 1, C#0; the vibrato reads $C331 + 2n, the low byte of the semitone above the note playing.
High byte of note 1, C#0 ($0127); the vibrato reads $C332 + 2n, the high byte of the semitone above the note playing.
Frequency table, notes 2-11: D0 ($0138, 18.3 Hz on PAL) to B0 ($020E, 30.9 Hz), low byte first. Octave 0 is never played: the patterns use notes 17 (F1) to 93 (A7).
Frequency table, octave 1: notes 12-23, C1 ($022D, 32.7 Hz on PAL) to B1 ($041B, 61.7 Hz), low byte first.
Frequency table, octave 2: notes 24-35, C2 ($045A, 65.4 Hz on PAL) to B2 ($0837, 123.5 Hz), low byte first.
Frequency table, octave 3: notes 36-47, C3 ($08B4, 130.8 Hz on PAL) to B3 ($106E, 247.0 Hz), low byte first.
Frequency table, octave 4: notes 48-59, C4 ($1168, 261.7 Hz on PAL) to B4 ($20DC, 494.0 Hz), low byte first. A4, note 57, is $1D46 = 440.1 Hz, the pitch the table is built on.
Frequency table, octave 5: notes 60-71, C5 ($22D0, 523.4 Hz on PAL) to B5 ($41B8, 988.0 Hz), low byte first.
Frequency table, octave 6: notes 72-83, C6 ($45A0, 1046.7 Hz on PAL) to B6 ($8370, 1976.0 Hz), low byte first.

Frequency table, octave 7: notes 84-95, C7 ($8B40, 2093.4 Hz on PAL) to A#7 ($F820, 3730.2 Hz), low byte first, and a last entry, note 95 = $FD2E, that is 3,806 Hz on PAL, 65 cents flat of B7 (a PAL B7 would need 67,280, more than 16 bits hold) and B7 exactly at the NTSC clock. The highest note the patterns play is 93, A7 (tune 0, pattern 32).
SID register offset of each voice, indexed by X: 0, 7, 14 ($D400, $D407, $D40E: voices 1, 2, 3).
Register offset of the voice being played (copied from music_voice_reg), the Y for its SID writes.

Pattern position of each voice (3 bytes): offset of the next byte to read in the pattern being played; 0 when a pattern ends.
Length counter of each voice (3 bytes): ticks left of the note sounding, from bits 0-4 of its first byte, counted down each tick; below 0 the next note is read.
First byte of the note sounding on each voice (3 bytes): bits 0-4 length, bit 5 tie, bit 6 rest, bit 7 instrument given; read again by the release, vibrato, drum and slide.
Control byte (waveform and gate) last written to each voice from its instrument (3 bytes); the release and the drum write it back with the gate bit cleared.
Note number (0-95) sounding on each voice (3 bytes); the vibrato and the octave effect look up its frequency again every frame.
Instrument number (0-16) of each voice (3 bytes), set by a note with bit 7 and kept until the next; a tune start does not reset it, and every voice's first note in the three tunes sets one.
Gate mask ANDed into the instrument's control byte when it is written: $FF for a note, $FE (gate off) for a rest.
Working copy of the first byte of the note being read, tested for bit 6 (rest) and bit 7 (instrument follows).
Working copy of the low byte of a frequency being written (note start and octave effect).
Saves the voice index X while X indexes the instrument table or holds the register offset; music_start_tune uses it as scratch for 2 x the tune number.
Working copy of the instrument's control byte, stored to music_control after the SID write.
Vibrato depth of the voice's instrument (byte 5), used as a shift count: the step is a semitone / 2^(depth+1); counted down by the shift loop.
Pulse speed of the voice's instrument (byte 6): with fx bit 3 the amount added to the pulse low byte each frame; otherwise bits 0-4 the sweep period in frames less 1 and bits 5-7 the step.
Vibrato step, low byte: the next semitone's frequency less the note's, shifted right depth + 1 times.
Vibrato step, high byte.
Frequency built by the vibrato, low byte: the note's plus phase x step.
Frequency built by the vibrato, high byte.
Vibrato phase for this frame, 0-3: the frame counter AND 7, folded (4-7 become 3-0).
Pulse sweep timer of each voice (3 bytes): counts frames down; below 0 it is reloaded with the pulse speed AND $1F and the pulse width takes a step.
Pulse sweep direction of each voice (3 bytes): 0 up, 1 down; turns when the pulse width's high nibble reaches $E going up or 8 going down.
Tempo counter: counts down every frame, reloaded from music_speed below 0; the frame on which it equals music_speed is a tick, when notes move on.
Tempo, frames per tick less 1. Never written: always 1, a tick every second frame (25 a second on PAL) in all three tunes.
Offset of the voice's instrument in music_instruments (instrument x 8), for the effects.
Driver state: $00 playing; $40 a tune has just been started (music_play resets the voices); $C0 stop requested (music_play silences the SID); $80 stopped (music_play does nothing).
Frequency high byte each voice's note started on (3 bytes); the drum and the slide count it down and write it to the SID.
Frequency low byte each voice's note started on (3 bytes); written by music_read_note, never read.
fx flags of the voice's instrument (byte 7): bit 0 drum, bit 1 slide, bit 2 octave, bit 3 pulse low-byte add.
Pulse sweep step for this frame: the pulse speed AND $E0.
Frame counter, + 1 on every music_play call, stopped or not, and 0 at a tune start; paces the vibrato (AND 7), the slide (bit 0) and the octave effect (AND 7).

Title picture's screen matrix: 1,000 bytes, one per character cell of the bitmap at $E000 (row r at $CC00 + 40r), read by the VIC in bank 3 through $D018 = $38 (title_irq_picture): the high nibble colours bit pair %01, the low nibble bit pair %10. 543 cells carry a high nibble of $E, light blue, that none of their pixels uses; the common values are $E8 (orange), $E9 (brown), $E7 (yellow), $E1 (white) and $91 (brown and white). Rows 23 and 24 ($CF98-$CFE7) are all 0. Loaded with the game; no code writes it. The sprite pointers that would follow at $CFF8-$CFFF are unused: the title shows no sprites.

Title picture: a multicolour bitmap of 8,000 bytes, $E000-$FF3F, in the RAM under the KERNAL ROM. The VIC reads it in bank 3 ($D018 = $38, title_irq_picture); the CPU, with $01 = $36, sees the KERNAL ROM at these addresses instead, and the label is named for the one CPU read: the random routine's LDA $E000,X at $2BAA takes ROM bytes $E000-$E0FF, not the picture. 25 rows of 40 cells of 8 bytes, row r at $E000 + 320r; each byte is four double-wide pixels: %00 the black background, %01 and %10 the colours in title_screen_matrix ($CC00), %11 colour RAM (filled from $AC00). Loaded with the game; no code writes it. This label's own bytes, cells 0-7 of row 0 ($E000-$E03F): the first flourishes at the top left of the logo.
Title picture, from cell 8 of row 0 to the end of row 2 ($E040-$E3BE; $E3BF, BASIC's RAM initialisation entry, is excluded): the upper half of the logo's THE MASTER OF in yellow and orange on black.

Title picture, row 3 and cells 0-8 of row 4 ($E3C0-$E543; $E544, the KERNAL's screen clear entry, is excluded): the lower half of THE MASTER OF in yellow and orange, and the dark grey edge of the cave roof at the right (cells 33-37).

Title picture, from cell 8 (byte 5) of row 4 to cell 15 of row 6 ($E545-$E7FF): the foot of THE MASTER OF, the top of MAGIC and the cave's outline in dark grey on both sides, with white and brown rock at the right.

Title picture, cells 16-23 of row 6 ($E800-$E83F): part of the top of MAGIC in yellow and orange. The label is named for the random routine's EOR $E800,Y at $2BB1, which reads the KERNAL ROM's bytes $E800-$E8FF, not the picture.
